name: Livestreaming
seo_title: Livestreaming and Kids: A Parent's Guide (2026)
seo_description: Livestreaming and kids: age rules for TikTok LIVE, YouTube, Instagram and Twitch, the risks of going live, and how to keep your child safe if they stream.
h1: Livestreaming and kids: a guide for parents
lead: Going live is a big draw for children: real-time chat, an audience and the dream of being a streamer. It's also the one place online where nothing can be taken back. Here's what the rules are and how to keep them safe.
answer: Most platforms say not alone, and not yet. TikTok only lets over-18s go live, YouTube needs an adult on camera with under-16s, and Instagram needs a parent's permission for under-16s. The risks are strangers in the chat, gifts used to pressure children, and things they can't undo.

sections.heading: The age rules for going live

subsections.heading: TikTok LIVE
body: You must be 18 to go live, and to send or receive gifts.

subsections.heading: YouTube
body: Since July 2025, under-16s can only stream with an adult visibly present on camera who manages the channel. Streams that break this can lose live chat or live features.

subsections.heading: Instagram
body: Teens under 16 need a parent's permission, through supervision, to go Live.

subsections.heading: Twitch
body: Users must be 13, and under-18s may only use Twitch with a parent or guardian's supervision.

subsections.heading: Strangers in the chat
body: Anyone watching can type to your child in real time, and offenders look for young streamers. Requests can start innocently ("do a twirl", "show your room") and escalate.

subsections.heading: Gifts and pressure
body: Gifts, donations and tips can be used to flatter a child and push them to do things on camera.

subsections.heading: It can't be undone
body: Viewers can record or screenshot a stream. Whatever happens live can be shared anywhere, forever.

subsections.heading: Giving too much away
body: A school jumper, a street outside the window or a name said aloud can tell a viewer where your child is.

subsections.heading: Watching streams
body: Live content is hard to moderate, so children watching streams can see violence, sexual content or cruelty before anyone removes it.

sections.heading: If your child streams
list: Stream from a shared room, with an adult nearby (and on camera on YouTube for under-16s)
Plan the background: no school logos, windows, post or anything with your address
Use a username that isn't their real name
Turn on chat filters, block words and use trusted moderators
Agree they'll end the stream straight away if anyone makes them uncomfortable
Never accept gifts in exchange for doing something on camera

sections.heading: Signs something's wrong
list: Secret streaming, or streaming late at night
Gifts, money or in-game items from viewers
A viewer who wants to talk privately or on another app
Seeming anxious or upset after going live

sections.heading: What parents can do
body: Watch a stream together, theirs or a streamer they like, and talk about the chat as well as the content. If they're desperate to stream, start with a recorded video you can check first. Live can come later, with you in the room.
list: "Who's your favourite streamer? What do you like about them?"
"What would you do if someone in the chat asked you to do something?"
"Could anyone work out where we live from your stream?"

teachers: Pupils who stream may be exposed to adults in real time without anyone else seeing. Listen for gifts from viewers, requests to move to private chats, or a pupil being recorded while live, and follow your safeguarding procedures.

faq.q: What age can you go live on TikTok?
faq.a: 18. TikTok only lets adults go LIVE, and only adults can send or receive gifts.
Only with an adult visibly present on camera who manages the channel. That rule started in July 2025.

faq.q: Can my teen go live on Instagram?
faq.a: Under-16s need a parent's permission through Instagram's supervision tools.

faq.q: Why is livestreaming risky for children?
faq.a: Strangers can talk to them in real time, gifts can be used to pressure them, and anything that happens can be recorded and shared.

help: Worried about something that happened on a stream? Childline is free and confidential on [0800 1111](tel:08001111), any time. Report suspected grooming to [CEOP](https://www.ceop.police.uk/). You are not alone.
